inlines.text: Identify which of the following vector pairs represent the

spec.sourceRegion: Third identification task, paired choices a–f
spec.description: Three columns and two rows. a: equal parallel northeast arrows. b: equal parallel arrows in opposite directions. c: unequal northeast arrows. d: arrows along the two sides of an open inverted V, pointing northeast and southeast. e: separated equal northwest arrows. f: longer northeast arrow above a shorter southwest arrow.
spec.mathematics: Equal vectors have both equal magnitude and equal direction; position does not affect equality.
spec.answerVisibility: All six pairs are permanent student-visible givens.

answer.worked: In pairs a and e, both vectors have the same magnitude and direction. Pair b has opposite directions; c has different magnitudes; d has different directions; f has different magnitudes and opposite directions.

Magnitude & direction: 3 cm northeast OR 3 cm at $45^\circ$ above the horizontal.

Variable notation: $\underset{\sim}{a}$, $\boldsymbol{a}$, or $\vec{a}$.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise three vector notations and distinguish valid scalar multiples and sums from scalar–vector addition.

content.prompt: Which of the following represent vectors?

answer.worked: Both $a$ and $b$ are scalars, so $5a+b$ is a scalar.
Multiplying a vector by 5 gives a vector. Adding the vector $\underset{\sim}{b}$ also gives a vector.
$-\underset{\sim}{c}$ is the vector $\underset{\sim}{c}$ multiplied by the scalar $-1$.
The bold letters represent vectors. Scalar multiplication and addition of these vectors give a vector.
The scalar 1 cannot be added to the vector $\underset{\sim}{f}$.
$\dfrac{\vec{a}}{5}=\dfrac{1}{5}\vec{a}$ is a scalar multiple of a vector.
The bold letter represents a vector, and multiplying it by the scalar $\dfrac{2}{3}$ gives a vector.
The vector $\boldsymbol{j}$ cannot be subtracted from the scalar 7.

children.prompt: Sarah walks 4 km North, then 3 km North. Draw a vector for her final displacement.

spec.description: Blank square grid with 12 columns and 10 rows; no axes or labels.
spec.mathematics: Space for a final displacement vector.

answer.short: An arrow pointing north, representing 7 km.
answer.worked: Place the 4 km north vector and the 3 km north vector tip to tail. Draw the resultant from the starting point to the final point: $4+3=7$ km north.

spec.description: Completed grid; one square represents 1 km and upward represents north.
spec.mathematics: Resultant is 7 km north.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Sarah walks 4 km North, then 3 km South. Draw a vector for her final displacement.

spec.description: Blank square grid with 12 columns and 10 rows; no axes or labels.
spec.mathematics: Space for a final displacement vector.

answer.short: An arrow pointing north, representing 1 km.
answer.worked: Place the 4 km north vector and the 3 km south vector tip to tail. The final point is $4-3=1$ km north of the starting point. Draw the resultant between these points.

spec.description: Completed grid; one square represents 1 km and upward represents north.
spec.mathematics: Resultant is 1 km north.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Sarah walks 5 km North, then 12 km East. Draw a vector for her final displacement.

spec.description: Blank square grid with 12 columns and 10 rows; no axes or labels.
spec.mathematics: Space for a resultant with 12 km east and 5 km north displacement.

answer.short: An arrow from the starting point to a point 12 km east and 5 km north.
answer.worked: Draw 5 km north followed tip to tail by 12 km east. Draw the resultant from the starting point to the final point. For example, use one square for 2 km: the final point is 6 squares right and 2.5 squares up.

spec.description: Complete solution grid with dashed tip-to-tail walking vectors and a solid resultant. One square represents 2 km; north is upward and east is right.
spec.mathematics: Resultant joins the starting point to the point 12 km east and 5 km north.

answer.worked:
For parallel vectors, $2\begin{pmatrix}3\\t\end{pmatrix}=k\begin{pmatrix}9\\12\end{pmatrix}$.

children.prompt:
Find the value of $p$ such that $p\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}$ is parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}7\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

Remember that parallel means $p\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}=k\begin{pmatrix}7\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

answer.worked:
$$p\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}3p+1\\-2p+4\end{pmatrix}=k\begin{pmatrix}7\\2\end{pmatrix}$$
$$\begin{aligned}3p+1&=7k\qquad(1)\\-2p+4&=2k\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Rearranging (2):
$$k=\frac{-2p+4}{2}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}3p+1&=\frac{7(-2p+4)}{2}\\2(3p+1)&=7(-2p+4)\\6p+2&=-14p+28\\20p&=26\\p&=\frac{13}{10}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain algebraically why the value of $p$ does not depend on the scalar multiple of $\begin{pmatrix}7\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

answer.short: Any nonzero scalar multiplying the target vector is absorbed into $k$, so the equation determining $p$ is unchanged.
answer.worked:
For a nonzero scalar $r$, write
$$\begin{aligned}\begin{pmatrix}3p+1\\-2p+4\end{pmatrix}&=k\left(r\begin{pmatrix}7\\2\end{pmatrix}\right)\\3p+1&=7kr\\-2p+4&=2kr\end{aligned}$$
Eliminating $kr$ gives $2(3p+1)=7(-2p+4)$, the same equation as in part a. Hence $p=\frac{13}{10}$ is unchanged.

answer.short: Nonzero scalar multiples point in the same or opposite direction, so they all give the same parallel condition.
answer.worked: Multiplying $\begin{pmatrix}7\\2\end{pmatrix}$ by a nonzero scalar changes its magnitude and may reverse its direction. Its line of direction stays the same. Therefore the value of $p$ needed for parallelism is unchanged.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the value of $q$ such that $\underset{\sim}{a}+q\underset{\sim}{b}$ is perpendicular to $\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

answer.worked:
$$\underset{\sim}{a}+q\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}3+q\\-2+4q\end{pmatrix}$$
A vector perpendicular to $\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\end{pmatrix}$ is parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-5\end{pmatrix}$ or $\begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
Using $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-5\end{pmatrix}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\begin{pmatrix}3+q\\-2+4q\end{pmatrix}&=k\begin{pmatrix}1\\-5\end{pmatrix}\\3+q&=k\\-2+4q&=-5k\end{aligned}$$
Substitute $k=3+q$:
$$\begin{aligned}-2+4q&=-5(3+q)\\-2+4q&=-15-5q\\9q&=-13\\q&=-\frac{13}{9}\end{aligned}$$
There is only one solution; using the opposite perpendicular direction gives the same value of $q$.

blocks.content:
Just like column vector notation, to add or subtract vectors, add or subtract each component.

$$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}&=x_1\boldsymbol{i}+y_1\boldsymbol{j}\\\underset{\sim}{b}&=x_2\boldsymbol{i}+y_2\boldsymbol{j}\\\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}&=(x_1+x_2)\boldsymbol{i}+(y_1+y_2)\boldsymbol{j}\end{aligned}$$

To multiply a vector by a scalar, multiply each component separately.

$$\underset{\sim}{a}=x\boldsymbol{i}+y\boldsymbol{j}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\lambda\underset{\sim}{a}&=\lambda(x\boldsymbol{i}+y\boldsymbol{j})\\&=\lambda x\boldsymbol{i}+\lambda y\boldsymbol{j}\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Given $\underset{\sim}{a}=6i-j$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=-2i+4j$, find the ratio $r:s$ if $r\underset{\sim}{a}+s\underset{\sim}{b}=0$.

answer.short: No defined ratio exists; the only solution is $r=s=0$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}r(6i-j)+s(-2i+4j)&=0\\6ri-rj-2si+4sj&=0\\(6r-2s)i+(-r+4s)j&=0\end{aligned}$$
Equate both components:
$$\begin{aligned}6r-2s&=0\\s&=3r\\-r+4s&=0\\-r+4(3r)&=0\\11r&=0\\r&=0\\s&=0\end{aligned}$$
Thus $r:s$ is undefined. The source answer $1:3$ satisfies only the $i$-component equation.

content.prompt: Given $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-12\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}-15\\-8\end{pmatrix}$, show that:

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}&=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-12\end{pmatrix}\\ 2\underset{\sim}{a}&=\begin{pmatrix}10\\-24\end{pmatrix}\\ \left|2\underset{\sim}{a}\right|&=\sqrt{10^2+(-24)^2}\\ &=26\\ \left|\underset{\sim}{a}\right|&=\sqrt{5^2+(-12)^2}\\ &=13\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS: }\left|2\underset{\sim}{a}\right|&=26\\ \text{RHS: }2\left|\underset{\sim}{a}\right|&=2(13)=26\end{aligned}$$
Hence, LHS $=$ RHS.

$$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{b}&=\begin{pmatrix}-15\\-8\end{pmatrix}\\ -\underset{\sim}{b}&=\begin{pmatrix}15\\8\end{pmatrix}\\ \left|-\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=\sqrt{15^2+8^2}\\ &=17\\ \left|\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=\sqrt{(-15)^2+(-8)^2}\\ &=17\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS: }\left|-\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=17\\ \text{RHS: }\left|\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=17\end{aligned}$$
Hence, LHS $=$ RHS.

$$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}&=\begin{pmatrix}5+(-15)\\-12+(-8)\end{pmatrix}\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}-10\\-20\end{pmatrix}\\ \left|\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=\sqrt{(-10)^2+(-20)^2}\\ &=10\sqrt5\\ \left|\underset{\sim}{a}\right|&=\sqrt{5^2+(-12)^2}\\ &=13\\ \left|\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=\sqrt{(-15)^2+(-8)^2}\\ &=17\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS: }\left|\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=10\sqrt5\approx22.36\\ \text{RHS: }\left|\underset{\sim}{a}\right|+\left|\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=13+17=30\end{aligned}$$
Hence, LHS $<$ RHS.

Using the magnitudes calculated in part c:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS: }\left|\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}\right|&=10\sqrt5\approx22.36\\ \text{RHS: }\left|\left|\underset{\sim}{a}\right|-\left|\underset{\sim}{b}\right|\right|&=|13-17|=4\end{aligned}$$
Hence, LHS $>$ RHS.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{AC}&=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}\quad(\triangle\text{ law})\\\overrightarrow{AC}&=(2\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b})+(2\underset{\sim}{a}-3\underset{\sim}{b})\\\overrightarrow{AC}&=4\underset{\sim}{a}-2\underset{\sim}{b}\\\overrightarrow{AC}&=2(2\underset{\sim}{a}-\underset{\sim}{b})\end{aligned}$$

Therefore $\overrightarrow{PR}$ is parallel to $\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}$ because it is a scalar multiple, with opposite direction.

answer.short: $\overrightarrow{PR}=\frac53\overrightarrow{PQ}$. The vectors are parallel and share point $P$, so $P,Q,R$ are collinear.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PQ}&=3\underset{\sim}{p}+9\underset{\sim}{q}\\&=3(\underset{\sim}{p}+3\underset{\sim}{q})\\\overrightarrow{PR}&=5\underset{\sim}{p}+15\underset{\sim}{q}\\&=5(\underset{\sim}{p}+3\underset{\sim}{q})\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt:
The diagram shows congruent parallelograms.

Let $\overrightarrow{BE}=\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\underset{\sim}{b}$.

Prove that $A,E,I$ lie on a straight line.

spec.description: Four congruent parallelograms in an oblique two-by-two grid. The A–E–I diagonal is not drawn. Vector arrows B to E and B to C carry under-tilde labels a and b.
spec.mathematics: Rows A,D,G; B,E,H; C,F,I are parallel and equally divided. Columns A,B,C; D,E,F; G,H,I are parallel and equally divided.

answer.short: $\overrightarrow{AE}=\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}=\overrightarrow{EI}$. These vectors are parallel and share $E$, so $A,E,I$ lie on a straight line.
answer.worked:
Corresponding sides of the congruent parallelograms give $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{EF}=\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{FI}=\overrightarrow{BE}=\underset{\sim}{a}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{AE}&=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BE}\\&=\underset{\sim}{b}+\underset{\sim}{a}\\\overrightarrow{EI}&=\overrightarrow{EF}+\overrightarrow{FI}\\&=\underset{\sim}{b}+\underset{\sim}{a}\end{aligned}$$
Thus $\overrightarrow{AE}=\overrightarrow{EI}$. They are parallel and share the common point $E$, so $A,E,I$ are collinear.

content.prompt: The triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(2\sqrt3,3)$, $B(3\sqrt3,4)$ and $C(2\sqrt3,5)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{OA}&=\begin{pmatrix}2\sqrt3\\3\end{pmatrix}\\\overrightarrow{OB}&=\begin{pmatrix}3\sqrt3\\4\end{pmatrix}\\\overrightarrow{OC}&=\begin{pmatrix}2\sqrt3\\5\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{AB}&=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}3\sqrt3-2\sqrt3\\4-3\end{pmatrix}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3\\1\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{CB}&=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OC}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}3\sqrt3-2\sqrt3\\4-5\end{pmatrix}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}|\overrightarrow{AB}|&=\sqrt{(\sqrt3)^2+1^2}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}|\overrightarrow{CB}|&=\sqrt{(\sqrt3)^2+(-1)^2}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: What type of special triangle is $ABC$? Why?

answer.short: Equilateral: all three sides have length $2$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{AC}&=\overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OA}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}2\sqrt3-2\sqrt3\\5-3\end{pmatrix}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}|\overrightarrow{AC}|&=\sqrt{0^2+2^2}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
$|\overrightarrow{AB}|=|\overrightarrow{CB}|=|\overrightarrow{AC}|$. Hence $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle, as each side has length $2$.

answer.short: $\overrightarrow{AD}=\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\11\end{pmatrix}$. One pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{AD}&=\overrightarrow{OD}-\overrightarrow{OA}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}-5-(-7)\\6-(-5)\end{pmatrix}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}2\\11\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{BC}&=\overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OB}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}10-8\\9-(-2)\end{pmatrix}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}2\\11\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$$
Hence $\overrightarrow{AD}=\overrightarrow{BC}$. Therefore $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, since one pair of opposite sides is equal in length and parallel.

Prove that MNC is a straight line.

spec.description: OC is horizontal with A its midpoint. Triangle OAB has N at the midpoint of AB and M two-thirds of the way from O to B. Only OC, OB and AB are drawn; the proposed line MNC is absent.
spec.mathematics: OA=AC; AN=NB; OM:MB=2:1. All six point labels and both marked interior points are retained.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question figure; no proof vectors or proposed collinear line are supplied.

answer.short: $\overrightarrow{MN}=-\frac13(\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y})$ and $\overrightarrow{MC}=-\frac43(\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y})=4\overrightarrow{MN}$. These vectors are parallel and share M, so M, N and C are collinear.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{AB}&=2\underset{\sim}{x}\\\overrightarrow{OB}&=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AB}\\\overrightarrow{OB}&=\underset{\sim}{y}+2\underset{\sim}{x}\\\overrightarrow{MN}&=\overrightarrow{MB}+\overrightarrow{BN}\\\overrightarrow{MN}&=\frac13(2\underset{\sim}{x}+\underset{\sim}{y})-\underset{\sim}{x}\\\overrightarrow{MN}&=-\frac13(\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y})\\\overrightarrow{MC}&=\overrightarrow{MO}+\overrightarrow{OC}\\\overrightarrow{MC}&=-\frac23(2\underset{\sim}{x}+\underset{\sim}{y})+2\underset{\sim}{y}\\\overrightarrow{MC}&=-\frac43\underset{\sim}{x}+\frac43\underset{\sim}{y}\\\overrightarrow{MC}&=-\frac43(\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y})\\\overrightarrow{MC}&=4\overrightarrow{MN}\end{aligned}$$
The vectors $\overrightarrow{MN}$ and $\overrightarrow{MC}$ are parallel and share the common point M. Therefore M, N and C lie on a straight line.

content.prompt:
The triangle $PQR$ is shown. $M$ is the midpoint of $QR$.

$\overrightarrow{PR}=\underset{\sim}{x},\quad \overrightarrow{PQ}=\underset{\sim}{y}$.

$\overrightarrow{PO}:\overrightarrow{OM}=3:2$.

$\overrightarrow{PN}$ can be written in the form $k\underset{\sim}{x}$.

Work out the value of $k$.

spec.description: Outline triangle PQR with horizontal PR, Q above, midpoint M on QR, N on PR, and segments PM and QN intersecting at O. All six labels are retained. No arrowheads, midpoint ticks or numerical dimensions.
spec.mathematics: M=(Q+R)/2; O=P+(3/5)(M-P); N is the intersection of QO with PR. Coordinates implement these relationships without printing additional givens.
spec.answerVisibility: All geometry is supplied in the question; no solution annotations or scalar value are shown.

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PR}&=\underset{\sim}{x},\quad \overrightarrow{PQ}=\underset{\sim}{y}\\\overrightarrow{QR}&=\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y}\\\overrightarrow{QM}&=\frac12(\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y})\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PM}&=\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QM}\\\overrightarrow{PM}&=\underset{\sim}{y}+\frac12(\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y})\\\overrightarrow{PM}&=\frac12(\underset{\sim}{x}+\underset{\sim}{y})\end{aligned}$

Since $PO:OM=3:2$,

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PO}&=\frac35\left[\frac12(\underset{\sim}{x}+\underset{\sim}{y})\right]\\\overrightarrow{PO}&=\frac3{10}(\underset{\sim}{x}+\underset{\sim}{y})\end{aligned}$

Since $Q,O,N$ are collinear, write $\overrightarrow{QO}=m\overrightarrow{QN}$.

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PO}&=\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QO}\\\overrightarrow{PO}&=\overrightarrow{PQ}+m\overrightarrow{QN}\\\frac3{10}(\underset{\sim}{x}+\underset{\sim}{y})&=\underset{\sim}{y}+m(k\underset{\sim}{x}-\underset{\sim}{y})\\\frac3{10}\underset{\sim}{x}+\frac3{10}\underset{\sim}{y}&=mk\underset{\sim}{x}+(1-m)\underset{\sim}{y}\end{aligned}$

Comparing coefficients:

$\begin{aligned}mk&=\frac3{10}\\1-m&=\frac3{10}\\m&=\frac7{10}\\k&=\frac37\end{aligned}$

content.prompt:
If $\mathbf{u}=2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$, the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{u}$ is:

$\text{A. }\frac{1}{13}(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$
$\text{B. }\frac{1}{5}(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$
$\text{C. }\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$
$\text{D. }\sqrt{13}(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$
[1]

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
|\mathbf{u}| &= \sqrt{2^2+3^2} \\
&= \sqrt{13}
\end{align*}$$
The unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{u}$ is:
$$\begin{align*}
\hat{\mathbf{u}} &= \frac{\mathbf{u}}{|\mathbf{u}|} \\
&= \frac{2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{13}} \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})
\end{align*}$$
Correct answer: C.

content.prompt: Consider $\mathbf{a} = 4\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = -2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the direction of $\mathbf{b}$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Since $\mathbf{b}=(-2,3)$ is in the second quadrant:
$$\begin{align*}
\tan\alpha &= \frac{3}{2} \\
\alpha &= \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) \\
&\approx 56.31^\circ \\
\theta &= 180^\circ - 56.31^\circ \\
&\approx 123.69^\circ
\end{align*}$$
Therefore the direction is $124^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find scalars $k$ and $l$ such that $k\mathbf{a} + l\mathbf{b} =\begin{pmatrix}10 \\ -2\end{pmatrix}$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
k\begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{pmatrix} + l\begin{pmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{pmatrix} &= \begin{pmatrix}10 \\ -2\end{pmatrix} \\
\begin{pmatrix}4k - 2l \\ k + 3l\end{pmatrix} &= \begin{pmatrix}10 \\ -2\end{pmatrix}
\end{align*}$$
Hence:
$$\begin{align*}
4k - 2l &= 10 \\
k + 3l &= -2
\end{align*}$$
From $4k - 2l = 10$:
$$\begin{align*}
2k - l &= 5 \\
l &= 2k - 5
\end{align*}$$
Substituting into $k + 3l = -2$:
$$\begin{align*}
k + 3(2k - 5) &= -2 \\
7k - 15 &= -2 \\
7k &= 13 \\
k &= \frac{13}{7}
\end{align*}$$
Then:
$$\begin{align*}
l &= 2\left(\frac{13}{7}\right) - 5 \\
&= \frac{26}{7} - \frac{35}{7} \\
&= -\frac{9}{7}
\end{align*}$$

entries.description: Syllabus Content
ME1-12-02 operates with 2D and 3D vectors and uses 2D vectors to solve problems involving motion in two dimensions
Vector representation and notation
Define a vector as a quantity having both magnitude and direction
Associate vectors with directed line segments and recognise that a vector may have many directed line segments associated with it

Identify and use notation for vectors in both two dimensions and three dimensions, including \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\underset{\sim}{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), where \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is the vector with magnitude and direction those of the directed line segment from \(A\) to \(B\)

entries.description: Use notations \(|\mathbf{a}|\), \(\left|\underset{\sim}{a}\right|\) and \(\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right|\) to represent the magnitude of a vector
Describe a position vector as a vector with its tail at the origin
Represent vectors graphically with and without graphing applications
Recognise and use the fact that two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction to solve problems
Introduction to 2D vectors
Use Cartesian coordinates to represent points in 2-dimensional (2D) and 3-dimensional (3D) space with and without graphing applications
Use the midpoint and distance formulas in two dimensions and three dimensions

Identify that, in three dimensions, all points on the \(xy\)-plane have a \(z\)-coordinate of 0, and deduce similar properties for points on the \(xz\) and \(yz\)-planes and thus the equations of the three coordinate planes
Define the zero vector \(\mathbf{0}\), written as \(\underset{\sim}{0}\), as the vector with zero magnitude and no direction
Define unit vectors as vectors of magnitude 1
Recognise and use \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{\hat{a}}\) as the notation for the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}\)
Define the standard perpendicular unit vectors \(\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{j}\) in two dimensions and \(\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) in three dimensions
Express 2D vectors in component form, \(x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}\); as an ordered pair, \((x,y)\); and in column vector notation \(\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}\)

entries.description:
A scalar quantity has only size, or magnitude.
E.g. Distance of school from home is 3 km.
Speed of a plane is 800 km/h.
Temperature, length, area, …

A vector quantity has magnitude and direction.
E.g. Displacement of school from home is 3 km at a bearing of 120°.
Velocity of a plane is 800 km/h at a bearing of 225°.
Acceleration, force, weight, …

A vector quantity is often used to represent movement or change.

entries.description: Given that \(\underset{\sim}{a}=\binom{2}{-2}\), \(\underset{\sim}{b}=\binom{-3}{-5}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{c}=\binom{24}{8}\), find the values of \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) such that \(\underset{\sim}{c}=\lambda_1\underset{\sim}{a}+\lambda_2\underset{\sim}{b}\).
entries.presentation: Prompt spans two lines. Preserve vector undertildes and space for simultaneous-equation working.

entries.description:
Supplied working, in order:
\(\underset{\sim}{c}=\lambda_1\underset{\sim}{a}+\lambda_2\underset{\sim}{b}\)
\(\binom{24}{8}=\lambda_1\binom{2}{-2}+\lambda_2\binom{-3}{-5}\)
\(\binom{24}{8}=\binom{2\lambda_1-3\lambda_2}{-2\lambda_1-5\lambda_2}\)
\(2\lambda_1-3\lambda_2=24\quad(1)\)
\(-2\lambda_1-5\lambda_2=8\quad(2)\)
Adding (1) and (2):
\(-8\lambda_2=32\)
\(\lambda_2=-4\)
Substitute \(\lambda_2=-4\) into (1):
\(2\lambda_1-3(-4)=24\)
\(2\lambda_1+12=24\)
\(\lambda_1=6\)

20p = 26
p = 13/10

entries.sourceLabel: Arithmetic with Vectors in Component Form
entries.description:
Just like column vector notation, to add or subtract vectors, add or subtract each component.
\mathbf a=x_1\mathbf i+y_1\mathbf j
\mathbf b=x_2\mathbf i+y_2\mathbf j
\mathbf a+\mathbf b=(x_1+x_2)\mathbf i+(y_1+y_2)\mathbf j
To multiply a vector by a scalar, multiply each component separately.
\mathbf a=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j
\lambda\mathbf a=\lambda(x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j)
\phantom{\lambda\mathbf a}=\lambda x\mathbf i+\lambda y\mathbf j

A = tan⁻¹(|y|/|x|)

In navigation scenarios, you may need to use true bearings instead of angle of inclination.

Supplied blue worked solution, in source order:
\(\overrightarrow{PR}=x,\ \overrightarrow{PQ}=y\)
\(\overrightarrow{QR}=x-y\)
\(\overrightarrow{QM}=\frac12(x-y)\)

\(\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QM}=\overrightarrow{PM}\)
\(y+\frac12(x-y)=\overrightarrow{PM}\)
\(\therefore\ \overrightarrow{PM}=\frac12(x+y)\)

\(\overrightarrow{PO}=\frac35(\frac12x+y)=\frac3{10}(x+y)\)
\(\overrightarrow{PO}=\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QO}\)
\(\overrightarrow{PO}=\overrightarrow{PQ}+m\times\overrightarrow{QN}\)
\(\frac3{10}(x+y)=y+m(kx-y)\)
\(\therefore\ \frac3{10}x+\frac3{10}y=mkx+(1-m)y\)
Comparing coefficients:
\(mk=\frac3{10}\)
\(1-m=\frac3{10}\)
\(m=\frac7{10}\)
\(\therefore\ k=\frac37\)

entries.description: Operating with vectors source heading preceding the eight inventoried syllabus bullets.
Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction.
Notation teaching continuation: use undertilde a; scalars cannot be added/subtracted with vectors; a scalar can multiply a vector.
Column Vector Arithmetic teaching: multiply each component by the scalar.
Column Vector Arithmetic teaching continuation: scalar multiplication distributes over vector addition.
Perpendicular-vector teaching continuation: multiply corresponding components and check their sum is zero.
Basis-vector teaching continuation: every vector is a sum of the horizontal and vertical unit vectors.
Existing parallelogram worked-example instruction: find the requested expressions in terms of vectors a and b.
